beats.text: "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains."
With that line, Rousseau opens his attack on the world we take for granted.
We imagine humans began free and happy, then built societies that bound them in rank and law.
But he doesn't tell us to smash every chain and return to the forest. That road is closed.
Instead he asks: can a chain ever be legitimate? Can we be bound and still be free?
Only, he says, if we obey laws we gave ourselves — the true meaning of the social contract.
So the question for any society is simple: did you choose these chains, or were they placed on you?

source_note: Quote: The Social Contract, trans. G. D. H. Cole (public domain).
